title: planr schema language v1
description: The planr schema language, version 1. It describes three things: a project's workflow file (.plan/workflow.yml), which declares the kinds of ticket the project uses and the verbs that move tickets between states; a ticket file's YAML frontmatter ('#ticket'); and the Planr-* trailers planr writes into each of its commits ('#commit'). Terms used throughout: a ticket is one file in .plan/tickets/, identified by its slug. A kind is a ticket's type, such as epic, story, or task. A state is a stage in a ticket's lifecycle, such as todo or done; planr computes it from the ticket's commits and never stores it. A verb is a named operation that moves a ticket from one state to another and makes exactly one commit. The version number tracks this language, not planr releases: it changes only when a key is added or removed or a key's meaning changes. This schema checks structure only; planr checks that each named kind and verb exists in the workflow. planr never fetches this document at runtime.

$schema.description: Declares which version of the planr schema language this file uses. Optional; planr treats a file without it as version 1. Cite the major-version alias (.../planr/v1/planr.schema.json) so compatible releases need no edit, or pin an exact version. Each version's $id is its exact, permanent URL, and the alias always points at the newest compatible version, so a document fetched through the alias carries an $id that differs from the URL used to fetch it. That is expected: the $id identifies the document. planr rejects a URL that names another major version with an explicit error.

verbs.description: The operations that change tickets. planr identifies a verb by its name together with 'applies-to', so a name may appear more than once when the entries apply to different kinds. That is how 'close' works one way for tasks and another for epics. Two entries with the same name must not apply to the same kind.

worktrees.description: Where planr creates worktrees for the unit. The unit is the kind whose tickets each get their own branch and worktree: the kind with a verb that declares 'worktree: create', usually task. The value is a path template, relative to the repository root unless absolute, in which $kind and $slug expand to the ticket's kind and slug. Worktrees are local and never committed, which is why this is a setting rather than part of a verb. The default keeps worktrees inside the repository, and so inside an agent's sandbox; use a path such as ../wt-$slug if a recursive file watcher is a problem.

identifier.description: A lowercase name, used for kinds, verbs, links, and states. Underscores are allowed so that names such as depends_on and in_progress fit.

verb-name.description: A verb's name: any identifier except 'new', which is reserved for ticket creation (see 'Planr-Verb').

slug.description: A ticket's identity. The slug names the ticket's file (<slug>.md) and its branch, has no numeric prefix, and contains no slash. A slug is never reused: archiving deletes the file but keeps the name, because every commit about the ticket records its slug, and reusing the slug would attach the old ticket's history to the new one. The length limit keeps file names and worktree paths within filesystem limits.

kinds.description: The kinds of ticket this project uses, arranged as a decomposition tree: each kind breaks down into the kinds below it, as an epic breaks down into stories and a story into tasks. A kind that groups tickets without breaking them down, such as a milestone, belongs in 'groups' instead. There is no 'unit' key. The unit is whichever kind has a verb that declares 'worktree: create', and it need not be the lowest kind in the tree.

oneOf.description: List form: kinds in order from outermost to innermost, each one containing the next. planr reads it as the equivalent object form.

parents.description: The kinds that may contain this one. An empty list marks a top-level kind. A ticket still has at most one parent; listing several kinds here lets that parent be any one of them.

oneOf.description: Object form: each kind lists the kinds that may contain it. Use it when a kind may sit under more than one kind of parent.

inverse.description: The name of the list of tickets in a group, such as 'members' for a milestone. planr builds the list from the member tickets' own fields and never stores it on the group ticket.

groups.description: Kinds that group tickets rather than breaking them down, such as a milestone. Each entry declares two things: a kind of ticket, the group itself, with its own lifecycle; and a field of the same name that other tickets set to join the group, as in 'milestone: v1-launch'.

cardinality.description: 'one' means the field holds a single target, changed with the 'set' operation. 'many' means it holds a list, changed with 'add' and 'remove'. planr writes a list one target per line, so two branches that add different targets merge without a conflict.

semantics.description: What the link means to planr. With 'rollup', a container closes only when its children have finished. With 'gate', a verb waits until every target is done. 'group' groups tickets without either effect, and 'info' is informational only. A [[slug]] link in a ticket's body is prose, not a link field, and is not declared here.

edges.description: Typed links between tickets, beyond the two that are built in. 'parent' is a single link that rolls up: a container closes only when its children have finished. 'depends_on' is a list of links that gate: a verb waits until each target is done.

body.description: The text a new ticket of this kind starts with. Leave out any section a verb requires, such as the Validation section 'submit' checks for. The check only tests that the section exists, so a body that already had it would pass the check before any work was done.

initial.description: The state a new ticket of this kind starts in. planr usually works this out: the starting state is the one state that some verb moves a ticket out of and no verb moves a ticket into. Declare it when a verb moves tickets back into the starting state, as 'yield' moves a task back to 'todo', because then no state qualifies.

templates.description: Per-kind scaffolding for 'new', plus the initial state where planr cannot derive it.

require.description: A precondition evaluated before any side effect. The vocabulary is three reserved structural operators combined by implicit AND. Every predicate is a pure graph fact, so it is derivable, cacheable, and reusable by lint as a standing invariant. Note that predicates are structural only, never semantic judgment; planr may check that a ticket is in the approved state, never whether the work is actually acceptable.

self.description: Checks on the ticket itself, such as 'status: approved'. Here 'status' is the ticket's computed state, not a stored field.

neighbors.description: Checks that every ticket at the other end of a link is in a given state, such as 'children: terminal' or 'depends_on: done'. There is no 'any' and no count. A dependency asks for 'done' because the work must have succeeded, while a container asks its children for 'terminal' (done or abandoned) because an abandoned child is a decision already made.

sections.description: Named sections that must be present in the ticket body, e.g. Validation.

content-step.description: An edit to the ticket file. Content steps change files only; the verb's 'base' and 'effect' decide which branch the commit is built on and which branch moves. All of a verb's content steps go into its one commit.

oneOf.description: Delete the ticket file. This is what archiving means: the file leaves the tree, the ticket keeps its final state, and git history keeps everything else.

body.description: The section's text. $message expands to the message given on the command line.

oneOf.description: Add a named section to the ticket body, such as a reviewer's findings. Use it for notes that someone must act on; other commentary belongs in the commit message.

Set, add to, or remove from a link field on the ticket. planr writes only the ticket's own fields; the reverse list on the other ticket is computed. planr checks that the target exists, that the two kinds may be linked, that the link creates no cycle, and that the operation fits the field's cardinality.

edge-assignment.description: One link field mapped to its target, usually $target, which expands to the slug given on the command line.

verb.description: One operation on a ticket, making exactly one commit. Some verbs change no file at all, and their commit message records the whole operation. planr builds the commit on 'base', puts any content steps in it, and then applies it as 'effect' says, so the keys have no order to declare.

applies-to.description: The kinds this verb works on. It also defines what each kind can do: an epic cannot be claimed because no 'claim' verb applies to epics.

from.description: The source state. Structural, and what makes each kind's sub-machine well-formed and 'terminal' derivable. Every progression verb that is the sole exit of its source state must declare it. Omitting it means 'any non-terminal state' and is reserved for a verb like 'abandon', which is never a sole exit and so cannot freeze a state. 'require' adds a precondition; it never substitutes for 'from'.

to.description: The state the ticket is in after this verb. Omit it for verbs that change no state, such as link edits. planr computes a ticket's state from its commits; nothing stores it.

content.description: The edits this verb makes to the ticket file, all in its one commit. May be empty: 'claim', 'submit', and closing a task edit no file, and their commit message records the whole operation. A verb with no content should have a 'require'; otherwise it records progress without checking anything.

base.description: The branch the verb's commit is built on. 'home' is the ticket's integration branch, which is trunk. 'own' is the ticket's branch, plan/<kind>/<slug>. planr builds the commit without checking out a branch, so a branch checked out in another worktree is no obstacle.

effect.description: The one branch this verb moves. 'advance' moves the base branch to the new commit. 'create' creates the ticket's branch at the new commit, and fails if the branch already exists, so two agents claiming one ticket at once cannot both succeed. 'merge' merges the new commit into trunk, so the ticket's final state and its work arrive together and one revert undoes both. 'ticket-only' merges the ticket file but not the work: trunk's files stay as they were apart from the ticket, and the merge records the ticket's branch as a parent, so the branch's commits stay in history and the branch can be deleted without losing them. No effect destroys work; deleting a branch outright is left to git.

retain-ref.description: With effect 'merge', keep the ticket's branch after merging instead of deleting it. The commits are reachable from trunk either way; keep the branch only if something outside planr, such as a code review on a forge, still needs it.

worktree.description: Creates or removes a worktree for the ticket's branch. The kind with a verb that declares 'create' is the unit. Both actions are safe to repeat: removing a worktree that does not exist does nothing, so re-running a verb after a partial failure completes it.

hook.description: Runs a project script. It is kept out of the common path so that an agent can read a verb and know what it does, and it is never allowed inside 'require', which stays a pure check.

allOf.$comment: A ref can only be cut from the integration ref the ticket already lives on.
Only a ticket's own ref can be integrated into its home, so base must be stated explicitly.
A ticket-only merge builds its tree from home and takes the ticket from the branch, so home is the base.

A worktree needs a ref that survives the step, not merely one that exists when the verb is checked. `effect: create` cuts one; `base: own` requires an existing one, which is how a yielded ticket is re-dispatched. But `merge` and `ticket-only` RELEASE the ticket's ref as part of the effect, so `base: own` alone is not sufficient -- pairing `worktree: create` with `merge` validates a ref and then deletes it, leaving a worktree pointing at a branch that no longer exists. See docs/semantics.md section 2.1.

ticket.title: planr ticket frontmatter
ticket.description: The YAML frontmatter of a ticket file. It holds only what git cannot supply: the ticket's kind, its title, and its links. planr computes the ticket's state from its commits, reading each commit under the workflow in force when it was made.

kind.description: Must name a kind in the project's workflow. It cannot change once the ticket is claimed, because the ticket's branch name, plan/<kind>/<slug>, includes it.

parent.description: The slug of the ticket that contains this one. Null or absent for a top-level ticket.

depends_on.description: The tickets this one waits on. planr writes the list one slug per line, so two branches that add different dependencies merge without a conflict.

status.description: Not allowed. planr computes a ticket's state from its commits, and a stored copy would stop matching them as soon as the workflow changed.

id.description: Not allowed. The slug is the ticket's identity.

created.description: Not allowed. The first commit of the ticket's file records when it was created.

updated.description: Not allowed. The latest commit of the ticket's file records when it was updated.

additionalProperties.description: Group membership and project-defined link fields, such as milestone. A single link is a string; a list of links is a block list.

commit.title: planr commit trailers
commit.description: The Planr-* trailers of a planr commit, as parsed key-value pairs. planr writes them as git trailers (see git-interpret-trailers), with exactly one Planr-Verb; JSON Schema can describe the parsed pairs but not that encoding. The subject line is conventionally 'plan: <verb> <slug>'. A commit records no workflow version: the workflow file lives in the same history, so the commit's own tree holds the workflow that applied when it was made, and a branch's commits are read under the workflow its author could see.

Planr-Verb.description: The verb this commit records. 'new' is not a verb: it marks the commit that created the ticket, and planr reads a ticket's history back to that commit and no further, which is why no verb may be named 'new'. Some verbs make identical file changes ('approve' and 'request-changes' both add a Review section), so this trailer is the only record of which one ran. This schema checks the name's form; planr checks that it names a verb in the workflow.

Planr-Ticket.description: The slug of the ticket this commit acts on. planr records it rather than inferring it from the files the commit changes, so a ticket's history survives renames, and a commit that deletes the ticket file still names its ticket.
